criteria.label: Full runtime self-hosts
criteria.description: The agent loop and execution runtime can run on infrastructure the operator controls; an SDK alone does not count.

criteria.label: First-party chat gateways
criteria.description: The compared runtime connects directly to chat services rather than requiring a separate application for every channel.

criteria.label: Multiple model routes
criteria.description: The runtime supports more than one model route or provider without replacing the agent architecture.

criteria.label: Durable cross-session memory
criteria.description: The runtime offers memory that can survive a process or session boundary. This says nothing about whether recall is automatic or safe.

criteria.label: Tool isolation is the default
criteria.description: Tool implementation starts without ambient host files, processes, network, environment, or credentials. Optional sandbox modes receive a partial mark.

criteria.label: Effect authority is separate
criteria.description: A process or managed service outside model orchestration owns the final permission transition and privileged effect execution.

criteria.label: Static policy names each action
criteria.description: A deterministic rule outside the prompt decides whether a named action may run. Broad runtime roles or an optional shell allowlist count only partially.

criteria.label: Credentials enter outside tool code
criteria.description: The runtime can present a service credential after tool code has formed its request, without placing the value in the prompt or tool implementation.

criteria.label: Each call has a hard I/O envelope
criteria.description: Trusted state binds destinations, methods or storage scope, call counts, byte ceilings, and a deadline to one operation. General quotas count only partially.

criteria.label: Tools ship as isolated portable artifacts
criteria.description: A reusable tool implementation ships as a sandboxed, host-architecture-independent artifact with an inspectable host interface—not as trusted in-process plugin code.

criteria.label: Permission and result share a durable record
criteria.description: Durable metadata correlates the actor, permission decision, attempted action, and terminal result. Traces or general cloud API logs count only partially.

selfHost.note: Four installable executables and a multi-architecture image.

channels.note: Slack, Discord, Telegram, WhatsApp, local socket, and terminal console.

models.note: OpenAI-compatible endpoints plus an isolated ChatGPT subscription route.

memory.note: Bounded in-process replay plus optional broker-owned on-demand durable chat memory.

defaultIsolation.note: The shell has no OS underneath; providers begin import-free or receive only an exact Dekopon host interface.

separateAuthority.note: dekopond and the console propose; dekopon-brokerd alone authorizes and executes effects.

staticActionPolicy.note: Cedar decides named actions; separate constraint sets bind execution.

hiddenCredentials.note: The native HTTP engine injects a destination-bound value after guest-header validation.

hardEnvelope.note: One authorization binds host or storage scope, calls, bytes, fuel, memory, and deadline.

portableArtifact.note: Providers are WebAssembly Components with versioned WIT imports and fresh Wasmtime stores.

durableAudit.note: Hash-linked metadata joins identity, Cedar decision, execution outcome, and evidence.

selfHost.note: The Gateway installs on operator-owned macOS, Linux, Windows, containers, and companion devices.

channels.note: First-party integrations include WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Signal, iMessage, and others.

models.note: Hosted and local model providers share the Gateway runtime.

memory.note: Workspace Markdown, SQLite-backed search, semantic recall, and optional memory plugins.

defaultIsolation.note: Official docs say sandbox mode defaults to off and main-session tools run on the host unless configured otherwise.

separateAuthority.note: The Gateway owns the model runtime, tool policy, credentials, plugins, and most execution inside one operator trust domain.

staticActionPolicy.note: Tool policy and host-exec allowlists are deterministic, but they are not a universal per-integration effect policy and trusted defaults can allow host exec.

hiddenCredentials.note: SecretRefs, sentinels, and an opt-in destination-bound egress proxy reduce exposure; native plugins still share Gateway process privileges.

hardEnvelope.note: Sandbox network settings, tool policy, approvals, and tool-specific timeouts exist, but no one envelope covers every effectful integration.

portableArtifact.note: Plugins load in-process as trusted code; skills and package installs do not form an isolated component ABI.

durableAudit.note: A bounded metadata-only SQLite audit ledger and decision receipts exist, but writes are best-effort and the ledger is not authorization evidence or a compliance archive.

selfHost.note: Runs locally, in Docker, over SSH, and on several remote or serverless terminal backends.

channels.note: The gateway advertises Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, email, and CLI.

models.note: Supports Nous Portal, OpenRouter, OpenAI, custom endpoints, and other providers.

memory.note: Persistent memory, session search, user modelling, and skill learning are first-class features.

defaultIsolation.note: The security policy says the default terminal backend executes on the host; OS-level terminal or whole-process isolation is an operator choice.

separateAuthority.note: The Python agent process owns model orchestration, plugins, credentials, hooks, and ordinary tool dispatch.

staticActionPolicy.note: Command allowlists and approval prompts catch mistakes, but the project explicitly calls them in-process heuristics rather than a security boundary.

hiddenCredentials.note: Child environments strip credentials by default and OpenShell can inject from a Provider store; in-process plugins can still read agent credentials.

hardEnvelope.note: Docker, SSH, cloud sandboxes, or OpenShell can bound selected execution paths; no universal per-tool effect envelope applies in the default runtime.

portableArtifact.note: Skills, plugins, MCP servers, Python dependencies, and terminal backends are reviewed operator code rather than one isolated provider artifact.

durableAudit.note: Official sources reviewed here describe logs and install review, but do not establish a durable permission-to-effect audit record.

runtimes.name: Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic
runtimes.scope: Maintenance mode · existing customers · AgentCore excluded

selfHost.note: AWS operates the managed orchestration runtime; custom software using Bedrock APIs is a different scope.

channels.note: The native surface is an API and console test interface; chat or voice channels come from an application or another AWS service.

models.note: An agent selects from the Bedrock model catalog frozen for Agents Classic on 30 July 2026.

memory.note: Optional summarized memory can retain sessions under a memory ID for up to 365 days.

defaultIsolation.note: Built-in Code Interpreter is managed; action code normally runs in adjacent Lambda or in the caller after return-control.

separateAuthority.note: IAM and the service role sit outside model reasoning, but Bedrock Agents has no documented per-effect broker equivalent.

staticActionPolicy.note: Action-group schemas, IAM, and optional user confirmation constrain execution without forming one per-call action policy.

hiddenCredentials.note: The agent uses an AWS service role; Lambda or the return-control application owns action-specific credentials.

hardEnvelope.note: Public docs reviewed here do not establish customer-authored destination, byte, call-count, and deadline bounds for each action.

portableArtifact.note: The extension unit is action-group configuration plus Lambda or caller code, not a portable isolated provider component.

durableAudit.note: InvokeAgent traces and optional CloudTrail data events exist, but they do not document one durable permission-and-remote-effect receipt.

selfHost.note: Open-source ADK applications can run on chosen infrastructure; Agent Platform Runtime, Memory Bank, and managed services stay on Google Cloud.

channels.note: Production chat and voice surfaces require a custom client or an adjacent Google product.

models.note: ADK is Gemini-first and supports other model adapters; managed-runtime feature parity varies.

memory.note: Managed sessions and Memory Bank store conversational state and long-term user facts.

defaultIsolation.note: Managed Code Execution uses an isolated sandbox, but that does not establish the same boundary for every ADK tool or agent process.

separateAuthority.note: IAM and service accounts live outside model reasoning, but they govern cloud resources rather than every model-selected tool call.

staticActionPolicy.note: IAM Conditions can narrow agents, sessions, and memory resources; no universal per-tool action policy was established.

hiddenCredentials.note: Workload identity, API keys, OAuth, and adjacent Secret Manager can hold credentials; no universal broker-late injection boundary was established.

hardEnvelope.note: Managed sandboxes and service quotas apply to some execution, not one customer-authored envelope around every tool call.

portableArtifact.note: ADK tools, OpenAPI tools, MCP servers, and deployed agents do not form one isolated cross-runtime provider artifact.

durableAudit.note: Cloud Trace, Logging, and audit services provide operational evidence without one documented permission-to-effect receipt.
